subject: storytime
title: The Emperor's New Clothes
about: Hans Christian Andersen's tale of an emperor who pays two tricksters for magic clothes that only clever people can see, parades through town in his underthings because nobody wants to look foolish, and is finally set straight by a child who says what everyone can see. First graders find it very funny, and this telling keeps it kind: the emperor laughs at himself, and the ending says plainly that it is brave to say what is true. It is a public-domain story retold here in first-grade words, five pages long.
tip: Ask why the grown-ups said the clothes were lovely, and why the child did not.

book.author: Hans Christian Andersen (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: Magic clothes nobody can see, and a child who says so.

passage.text:
Once there was an emperor.
He loved new clothes more than anything.
He had a coat for every hour of the day.
One day, two tricksters came to town.
"We can weave the finest cloth," they said.
"It is magic cloth."
"Only clever people can see it."
"I must have it!" said the emperor.
He gave them a big bag of gold.
***
The tricksters sat at an empty loom.
They moved their hands back and forth.
But there was no cloth at all!
The emperor sent a wise old man to look.
The man saw nothing.
"Oh no!" he thought.
"Maybe I am not clever."
So he said, "What lovely cloth!"
Everyone else said the same.
Nobody wanted to look foolish.
***
At last the tricksters said, "It is done!"
They pretended to dress the emperor.
He had nothing on but his underthings!
He looked in the mirror.
"Oh my, they fit so well!" he said.
Nobody wanted to look foolish.
The tricksters took the gold and slipped away.
Then the emperor went out for a parade.
***
The people lined the streets.
"What a fine coat!" they said.
"What a fine hat!"
Nobody wanted to look foolish.
Then a little child looked up.
"But he has nothing on!" said the child.
Everyone got very quiet.
Then someone giggled.
Then everyone laughed and laughed.
***
The emperor looked down.
He saw his underthings.
He turned red.
"Oh my, I look silly!" he said.
Then he laughed too.
"Ho, ho! The child is right!"
"That child is brave."
"I am glad someone told the truth."
He went home and put on his old coat.
It is brave to say what is true.

cards.q: What did the emperor love more than anything?
cards.note: A coat for every hour of the day; that is why the magic cloth was so tempting.

cards.q: Who did the tricksters say could see the cloth?
cards.note: There was no cloth at all; saying only clever people could see it kept everyone quiet.

cards.q: What did the emperor give the tricksters?
cards.note: He paid a big bag of gold for cloth that did not exist.

cards.q: Who said, 'But he has nothing on!'?
cards.note: Everyone else was afraid of looking foolish; the child just said what was there.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: Two tricksters arrive with a promise of magic cloth; everything else follows from that.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: He turned red, laughed at himself, and went home for his old coat.

cards.q: How did the emperor feel when he looked down?
cards.note: He turned red and said so himself, then laughed: a good way to handle a mistake.
Everyone saw the truth, but only the child was brave enough to say it.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'clever' mean?
cards.note: Clever means smart, quick to understand; nobody wanted to seem the opposite.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.
